SPECIFICATION FOR POWDERED TALC FOR CERAMIC INDUSTRY
0. FOREWORD
0.1 This Indian Standard was adopted by the Indian Standards~lnstitution
on 27 December 1982, after the draft finalized by the Ceramicware Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 0.2 Talc, a hydrated magnesium silicate, is one of the most common minerals used in the ceramic industry. It is very soft, being used as the standard of No. 1 hardness in Moh's scale. Mineral masses of the composition 3 Mg0.4 SiO,.H,O are known as talc, the impure varieties as soapstone and relatively purer massive varieties as steatite. Talc almost invariably contains some impurities like carbonates, iron oxide, gangue, etc, which, if present, impart a dark colo~u or produce spots or specks in the ware on firing. 0.3 In ceramic compositions talc provides a cheap source of magnesia; which while acting as a flux also imparts properties of high thermal shock resistance, high electrical resistance at elevated temperature, and low dielectric loss and low power factor. The latter two being of great significance when currents of high frequency are applied. Therefore, talc finds use in the manufacture of low loss electro-ceramic insulators, low expansion cordierite bodies, tiles and glazes. 0.4 For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS : 2-1960*. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.
---e-1-

1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard prescribes requirements and methods of sampling and test for talc suitable for use in ceramic insulator industry and pottery industry.

OF LOSS ON IGNITION

F3.1 Procedure - Transfer one gram of the test sample to a weighed platinum crucible and introduce it into a muffle furnace and slowly raise the temperature to 950 to 1 000�C. After about 30 minutes, remove the crucible and cool in a desiccator and weigh. Repeat the ignition and cooling to obtain constant mass. F-3.2 Calculation M x 100 Loss on ignition, percent by mass =M where M, = loss in mass in g on ignition, and M = mass in g of the sample taken for the test. F-4. DETERMINATION OF SILICA

F-4.0 On&se of the Method - The sample is decomposed by fusion with sodium carbonate and extracted with acid. Silica is then determined gravimetrically by dehydration and baking followed by hydrofluorization. The residual silica in the filtrate is determined photometrically using molybdenum blue method. a) Fuse 0.200 g of pure silica ( 99.8 percent ) in 5 g of sodiull\ carbonate in a platinum crucible. ISrm429-1982 F-4.2 Procedure FA.2.1 Decomposition of the Sample - Weigh accurately about 0.5 g of the finely ground and dried ( 105 to 110�C ) sample into a platinum crucible. Add 3 g of sodium carbonate; after mixing intimately, cover the dish with lid and heat over a Meker burner, slowly increasing the temperature with caution till the mixture fuses. Keep at this temperature for 10 minutes and finally heat till a clear melt is obtained. Remove from the burner and cool. Extract the melt in a porcelain dish first with water and then with ( 1 : 1 ) dilute hydrochloric acid. F-4.2.1.1 Add about 30 ml of ( 1 : 1 ) dilute hydrochloric acid and O-5 ml of dilute sulphuric acid. Cover the porcelain dish and allow to stand on a steam bath until disintewation of the melt is complete. Crush any large flakes with flattened end of a glass.rod. F-4.2.2 Gravimetric Determination of Insoluble Silica - Evaporate the solution in the porcelain dish to dryness and allow it to remain on the steam bath for another hour. Transfer the dish to an air oven maintained between 105 to 110�C and bake for one hour. Cool the dish and add 20 ml of ( 1 : 18 ) oric acid fbllowed by 30 ml of hot water. Stir the mixture dilute hydrp till solution 7 o soluble salts appears to be complete. Digest the mixture on a steam bath for 10 minutes without stirring. Filter through NO. 42 filter paper and rinse'the dish with ( 1 : 1 ) dilute hydrochloric acid scrubbing the basin with a rubber-tipped glass rod. Wash the precipitate five times with ( 1 : 19 ) hot dilute hydrochloric acid and then with hot water until free from chloride. Reserve the filterate and washings for photometric determination of residual silica. F-4.2.2.1 Transfer both the filter paper and precipitate to a tared platinum crucible. Ignite at a low temperature until the precipitate is free from carbonaceous matter and then heat in the muffle furnace at 1 050�C to constant mass ( one hour being normally suficient ). Cool in a desiccator and weigh recording the mass as M,. Moisten the contents of the cold crucible `with water, add five drops of dilute dulphuric acid and 10 ml of hydrofluoric acid. Evaporate to dryness on a hot plate or sand bath, in a fume cupboard, taking care to avoid spurting. F-4.2.2.2 Heat the crucible and the residue, cautiously at first, over a .gas flame until the disappearance of white fumes and finally for five mmutes in the furnace at 1 05O"C, cool in a desiccator and weigh recording the mass as M2.
NOTE - If the residue weighs more than 10 mg, repeat the treatment with dilute sulphuric acid and hydrofluoric acid, ignite, cool and weigh ( itplMt 1. Then fuse any residue with 0.5 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate, dissul vc in 10 1111 of ( 1 : 4 ) dilute hydrochloric acid and transfer quantitatively to the filtrate and washings reserved in F-4.2.2.

13

IS: 10429- 1982 F-4.2.3 Test Blank Solutiotz- Prepare a test blank solution using the same procedure and quantities of reagents as detailed from F-4.2.1 to F-4.2.2.2 but excluding the sample and dilute LIP to the mark in a 250-ml volumetric flask.
F-4.2.4 Photometric Determination oj' the Re,sidual Silica - Boil the filtrate and washings reserved in F-4.2.2 and reduce to about 200 ml. Transfer to a 250-ml volumetric fIask and make up to the mark with water. Fusion may, however, be omitled to avoid undue attack on platinum NOTEcrucible. F-4.2.4.1 Transfer 10 ml aliquot of the solution prepared in F-4.2.4 to a 50-ml volumetric flask. Also transfer 10 ml each of the test blank solution prepared in F-4.2.3 to five 50-ml volumetric flasks. Add to the five flasks 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 ml respectively of the standard silica solution. Then to all the flasks add 5 ml of EDTA solution, a drop of phenolphthalein solution and then dilute ammonia solution dropwise until the colour. changes to red. Then add 5 ml of ferric ammonium sulphate solution and dilute to about 30 ml with water ( the pH of the solutions should be 1 to 1.5). F-4.2.4.2 Add 5 ml of ammonium molybdate solution and allow to stand for 10 minutes. Then add 5 ml of oxalic acid solution followed immediately by 5 ml of ascorbic acid solution and dilute the volume to 50 ml. Allow the solution to stand for 30 minutes for development of full colour. F-4.2.4.3 Starting with the blank ( ` 0 ' ml ) solution transfer a suitable portion of the coloured solution one at a time to an absorption cell, record the photometric readings using the light band centred approximately at 810 nm. Prepare the calibration curve from these readings against concentration of silica in mg ( as SiO, ) . F-4.2.4.4 Similarly, transfer a suitable aliquot ofcoloured test solution IO the absorption cell and note the photometric reading for the test solution. (:onvert it to milligrams of silica by means of the calibration curve and calculate the silica content in grams ( M3 ) in 250 ml of solution prepared in F-4.2.4. F-4.3 Calculation

,\,I, = mass in g of crucible and contents before hydrofluoric acid treatment, .\I, = mass in g of crucible and residue after hydrofluoric acid treatment, MB = mass in g of silica present in 250 ml of solution prepared in F-4.2.4, and :%I = mass in g of sample taken for the lest in F-4.2.1. 14

F-5. DETERMINATION OF

ALUMINA

F-5.0 Outline of the Method - Aluminium is separated from the aliqiiot of solution prepared in F-4.2.4 as sodium aluminate by treatment with sodium hydroxide and is complexed quantitatively with EDTA by boiling with an excess of the reagent. The excess EDTA is back titrated with standard zinc solution at PH about 5.2 using xylenol orange indicator. The aluminium EDTA complex on boiling with ammonia fluoride liberates EDTA which when titrated with standard zinc solution gives the amount of aluminiuni present in the solution.
F-5.1 Reagents

F-5.2.1 Solution of the Sample - Weigh accurately about 2 g of the finely ground test sample ( F-l.1 ) in a platinum dish. Moisten the sample with 5 ml of water. Add 3 ml of dilute sulphuric acid and 20 mI of hydrofluoric acid and evaporate slowly to dryness on the sand bath or hot plate in a fume cupboard taking care to avoid spurting. Repeat the process with 10 ml of hydrochloric acid. Cool, add 2 ml of dilute sulphuric acid and evaporate as before. Heat the dry residue cautiously until fumes of sulphur trioxide cease. Raise the temperature to 1 000�C and ignite for five minutes. Cool and. fuse the residue with 1 g of sodium carbonate and dissolve in hydrochloric acid, cool and dilute to 250 ml in a volumetric flask. F-5.2.2 Transfer loo-ml aliquot of the solution prepared in F-5.2.1 to a SOO-ml beaker and nearly neutralize with sodium hydroxide solution. Add with constant stirring another 100 ml of sodium hydroxide solution containing 1 g of sodium carbonate dissolved in it. Allow to stand on a warm water bath for one hour. Finally cool to room temperature, transfer qltantitativeiy to a 250-m] volumetric flask and dilute up to the mark with water. Mix well and allow to stand for a few minutes. Filter through a filter paper previously washed with sodium hydroxide solution, collecting the filtrate in a beaker, rinsing the beaker first with a little filtrate.

F-7.0 Outline of the Method - In an aliquot of the sample solution, R,Os group elements are masked by triethanolamine, and calcium and magnesium are titrated with EDTA solution at PH 10 using eriochrome black T indicator. In another aliquot magnesium is precipitated out at pH 12 in the presence of triethanolamine and calcium is titrated with EDTA using Patton and Reader ( P & R ) indicator. Subtracting the titre value of calcium from that of calcium and magnesium, the titre value for magnesium us obtained. F-7.1 Reagenta Concentrated Jvitric Acid ( see IS : 264-1976* ).

IS : 19429 - 1982 the dish with a lid. F-S.0 General - Sodium and potassium conten' ,are determined with the help of a flame emission spectrophotometer " measuring the intensity @J of radiation emitted at 767 nm by potassium or *at 589 nm by sodium. For this purpose use may also be made of a filter type flame photometer. In both the cases, however, the intensity of radiation either at the specified wavelength, or through the relevant filter is compared with that obtained for simulated standard solutions prepared from potassium chloride and sodium chloride solutions.
NOTE - Water used in preparing standard solutions shall be double-distilled so that it does not produce deflection of the galvanometer when the instrument is set for full scale deflection for 10 ppm of potassium or 5 ppm of sodium concentration.

F-8.1 Apparatus
with arrangement for monoF-8.1.1 Flame Photometer -Provided chromatic light or a set of filters required for determination of potassium and sodium. The photometer comprises essentially a galvanometer, a photocell or tube and a photo-multiplier tube. Other accessories are an atomizer-burner ( or an atomizer and a burner ) fed with liquefied petroleum gas ( LPG ) and compressed air ( or oxygen, acetylene, etc ) in such a ratio that combustion of gas is complete. F-S.1.2 Burette - 50 ml nominal capacity for Class A accuracy (see IS : 1997-1967*). and graduated in 0.1 ml

One millilitre of these solutions are respectively equivalent to 70, 60, 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 ppm of potassium ( as K ). F-8.3 Setting up the Apparatus - Switch the instrument on and wait for its stabilization. Adjust the slit and wavelengths ( 767 nm for potassium or 589 nm for sodium) or place the filters in position as the case may be. F-8.3.1 Pour water in the spray cup, open its tap and turn the compressed air or oxygen on. Adjust the tap and pressure to establish atmoization of water in a fine spray. Open the gas tap and light the burner. Adjust gas, if necessary, to get complete combustion. Next switch the photocell on and adjust the indicator needle or the indicator light spot, as the case may be, to bring it to the ` zero ' position. 22

IS : lo429 - 1982 F-8.3.2 Atomize potassium ( 70 ppm, F-8.2.3.2 ) or sodium ( 50 ppm, F-8.2.2.2 ) solutions in place of water ( F-8.3.1 ) and adjust the deflection to full scale. Atomize water once again to check the indicator needle or light spot rests at ` zero `. If it shifts from ` zero ' again adjust it to ` zero `. Thus when the instrument reads ` zero ' with water and shows full scale deflection for 70 ppm K, or `20 ppm Na solution, it is ready for use.
NOTE 1 - Atomization of any solution should always be followed by atomization of double-distilled water till the indicator comes to zero position. NOTE 2 -Do not disturb the setting of the atomizer or l@rner so that rates of Row are constant for a series of deterrdinations.

F-8.4.2 Calibration Graph and Determination - Without disturbing the setting of the instrument, atomize standard potassium ( F-8.2.3.2 ) or in an ascending sodium ( F-8.2.2.2 ) .,olutions of different concentrations order and plot the readings of the indicator against concentrations and draw the graph. Next atomize the sample solution reserved in F-8.4.1 and note the deflection and calculate concentration of potassium or sodium as the case may be. G-l.3

Preparation of Test Pieces

G-1.3.1 For determination of ceramic properties, take out the body slip in a tray and allow to dry in an air oven up to a plastic consistency, cool and mix thoroughly. Extrude out test rods 19 mm in diameter and 150 mm long through a de-airing pug mill, with a vacuum of about 500 mm of mercury. Put shrinkage marks on the rods. ,411ow the test pieces to dry very slowly first in air and then in an air oven.

IS : 10429 - 1982 G-1.3.2 For determination of dielectric properties take out the body slip in a tray and allow to dry in an air oven at 110�C. Crush and grind the dried material to pass through a 250-micron IS sieve and mix with 5 percent moisture, 1 percent starch as binder and 0.5 percent wax as lubricant. Granulate the mixture by squeezing through a 1* 00-mm IS sieve. Make discs measuring 57 mm diameter and 3 mm thickness by pressing in a steel die at a pressure of 25.6 MPa. C-1.4 Fire the test pieces in an electric furnace with one Orton standard pyrometric cone No. 10.
